statement: In 12 healthy volunteers who had used MDA, or both MDMA and a classic psychedelic, before, one dose of MDA by mouth in hospital (1.4 mg/kg, 83 to 128 mg; study condition), compared not with MDMA in the same people but with MDMA data (1.5 mg/kg; study condition) from other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team, whose self-ratings and heart rate were recorded for 6 hours instead of the 8 recorded after MDA, was associated with effects that lasted longer, more visual and 'spiritual' effects, fewer anxious ones and a smaller rise in heart rate (Baggott et al., 2019). Because this comparison is across separate studies and not randomized, and the MDMA volunteers are not described (16 in some analyses, 12 in others), any of these differences may come from who was studied or how long they were watched rather than from the drugs. Length: at 6 hours no MDMA rating was still significantly above its dummy pill, whereas all five general drug-effect ratings still were after MDA (any drug effect 46.4 points above its dummy pill on a 0 to 100 scale, and 41.6 points above MDMA, at that hour); at 8 hours all but the bad-effect rating were still raised after MDA, a time at which MDMA was not recorded. Kind: on a 66-item altered-states questionnaire rated at 8 hours for the peak of the experience (12 people per drug), MDA was rated higher than MDMA on complex and elementary visual imagery and on spiritual experience, and only MDA raised 'audio-visual synesthesia' (sounds changing what is seen); MDMA was rated higher than MDA on anxiety, 'dread of ego dissolution' and impaired control and thinking, three scales on which MDA did not differ from its dummy pill; both drugs raised blissful state, 'oceanic boundlessness', visionary changes, insightfulness, a sense of unity, changed meaning of things perceived and feeling out of the body. Against its dummy pill MDA raised ratings of feeling close to others, as MDMA did against its own (the two did not differ significantly), while on a scale of social feelings only MDMA raised warmth toward others ('Affiliation'; no statistic printed). The authors' description of MDA as more inward and emotionally intense, and of MDMA as more outgoing, is their impression, without data. Heart and blood pressure: heart rate rose by 20 (± 3) beats a minute after MDA against 30.6 (± 4.5) after MDMA (p = 0.03), although the abstract and discussion call the rises similar; MDA's highest reading came from 8 hourly measurements and MDMA's from 6, and a longer window can only raise a maximum, so the window does not explain MDA's smaller rise (editors' reasoning); the highest systolic pressure rose by 33 and 31 mmHg and diastolic by 24 and 19 mmHg (difference p = 0.06). Unwanted effects: over the whole session, ratings of a bad drug effect were not significantly above either dummy pill (at 6 hours MDA's was), and ratings of feeling anxious or paranoid showed no significant effect of condition; the abstract calls MDA well tolerated, but the paper reports no adverse events at all, although its methods describe safety monitoring and a check two weeks later. MDA's half-life in blood averaged 10.9 hours (SD 4); the paper compares it with MDMA figures from another team's study, and its abstract and discussion disagree on whether the half-life explains the longer effects. The volunteers were screened, healthy and experienced, few of them women (number not given), in hospital, given one known dose each; MDA and its dummy pill came on consecutive days, with MDA still in the blood on the second day in the half who had the dummy pill second; nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not studied; people with heart disease were excluded, and the authors say the blood-pressure rises could matter for them. The paper did not ask why MDMA is more widely used than MDA. Its authors write, citing other papers, that MDA is often sold as 'ecstasy' in place of MDMA. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How is MDA different from MDMA? Only one lab study has compared them, and not in the same people. Twelve healthy volunteers who had used such drugs before took MDA and, on another day, a dummy pill in hospital, without knowing which; their results were set beside MDMA results from other people in the same team's earlier studies, who were watched for 6 hours instead of 8. MDA's effects seemed to last longer: they were still clearly there at 8 hours, while MDMA's had faded by 6. MDA brought more visions with eyes closed and more 'spiritual' feelings, and less anxiety and loss of control, than MDMA did; both made people feel close to others. Heart rate rose by about 20 beats a minute after MDA, against about 31 after MDMA, and top blood pressure by about 30 points with both. The paper calls MDA well tolerated but reports no side effects at all. Because the two drugs were tested on different people, watched for different times, these differences may not come from the drugs. Nobody took a second dose, and the study did not ask why MDMA is more popular.
population: 12 healthy, screened adult volunteers with earlier self-reported experience of MDA, or of both MDMA and a classic psychedelic such as LSD, and no drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine (mean age 27.8, SD 8; few women, number not given), studied during one hospital stay in San Francisco; MDMA comparison data from 12 to 16 other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team, not described in this paper

comparator: Placebo in the same 12 people on the day before or after (half in each order; how the order was set is not stated); for the drug comparison, racemic MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and its placebo given to other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team (not randomized against MDA; self-ratings and heart rate recorded to 6 hours instead of 8)

statement: In 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35; half had used a psychedelic before) who each took LSD (100 and 200 µg as labelled, in solution), psilocybin (15 and 30 mg, in capsules of the pure drug, not mushrooms) and a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in random, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions (study conditions), LSD compared with psilocybin made the effects last longer and raised heart rate more, while the higher psilocybin dose raised blood pressure and body temperature more; ratings of what the experience was like did not differ significantly between the higher psilocybin dose and either LSD dose on almost every scale, which in 28 people does not show that the experiences are the same (Holze et al., 2022). Length: from each person's 'any drug effect' ratings (a modelled curve, counted from and to 10% of the person's own peak), the effects lasted on average 5.6 hours (SD 2.2) after psilocybin 15 mg, 6.5 (2.4) after 30 mg, 9.3 (3.2) after LSD 100 µg and 11 (3.7) after 200 µg (both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses, p < 0.001); they began on average 0.4 to 0.6 hours after LSD and 0.8 hours after psilocybin, which the authors put down to LSD being a liquid and psilocybin a capsule, not to the drugs, and they say, without a formal test, that LSD's longer half-life in blood (about 4 hours, against about 2.5 for psilocin, the form psilocybin takes in the body) fully explains the longer duration. Kind: psilocybin 30 mg and either LSD dose did not differ significantly on any visual analogue scale or on any subscale of the main altered-states questionnaire (5D-ASC); LSD 200 µg was rated higher than psilocybin 30 mg only on 'ineffability' (how hard the experience was to put into words), and both LSD doses raised 'emotional excitation' on a mood scale more than psilocybin; the lower psilocybin dose gave lower peak ratings than the higher one on several scales. These are non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins, with most of the numbers in an online supplement that was not read, so the abstract's conclusion that the two drugs' effects do not differ beyond duration goes further than the tests can. Body: both drugs raised blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size against the dummy; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than LSD, and both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses; on the group's average curves the differences were modest (systolic pressure roughly 139 mmHg after psilocybin 30 mg against 131 to 133 after LSD and 118 to 120 on the dummy; temperature about 37.6 to 37.7 °C against 37.3 to 37.4 and about 36.7; heart rate about 76 to 82 beats a minute after LSD against about 72 after psilocybin 30 mg and 62 to 65 on the dummy; editors' reading of the figure, as the peak values are in the unread supplement). Unwanted effects: total scores on a list of complaints in the first 12 hours rose with all four active conditions against the dummy, and from 12 to 24 hours with the higher dose of each drug; within 48 hours, counted by drug, 4 people had a headache after psilocybin and 3 after LSD, 2 had low mood after each, 2 and 1 had nausea, and there was one migraine (LSD) and one nosebleed (psilocybin), with 9 flashback episodes in 5 people within 72 hours (5 after LSD, 4 after psilocybin; what was counted is not explained) and no severe adverse event. Blinding: the dummy was recognised in 96% of sessions, and although the paper says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, by its own percentages people named the right drug (either dose) in at least 64% of psilocybin 15 mg sessions, 86% of psilocybin 30 mg sessions, 78% of LSD 100 µg sessions and 79% of LSD 200 µg sessions (editors' calculation: correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug), so expectation may have shaped the ratings. How strongly people felt each condition varied widely from person to person (ranges in Table 1), and nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not tested. The study did not test which amounts of the two drugs match, and this answer gives none; the authors' figures on matching amounts rest on doses this study did not give. Three printed values for LSD 100 µg are impossible: two means in Table 1 and one in the pharmacokinetics paragraph lie outside their own ranges. The volunteers had little drug experience (at most 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs other than cannabis) and no personal or family history of major psychiatric illness, and were in a calm hospital room with an investigator; the LSD solution held about 15% less than its label (84.5 µg per 100 µg unit). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different? One careful lab study gave 28 healthy adults both LSD and psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, each on separate hospital days along with a dummy, in random order and without telling them which. The clearest difference was length: LSD's effects lasted about 9 to 11 hours on average, psilocybin's about 6 to 7. LSD also started a little sooner, which the authors put down to it being given as a liquid. Psilocybin's higher dose raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more, while LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints such as headaches, and nobody had a serious problem. Otherwise, the trips were rated alike on almost every scale. But not finding a difference in 28 people does not prove there is none, and by the study's own figures people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. The study used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms, and did not test which amounts of the two drugs match.

statement: In 9 healthy young men who had taken MDMA before (5 to 100 times; on average 26), MDMA (100 mg) taken with alcohol (0.8 g/kg), compared with each drug alone and with a dummy in the same men, one week apart, in random order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a quiet laboratory room (study conditions), was associated with feeling as drunk as with alcohol alone but less sleepy, with test scores that fell about as far at their worst as with alcohol alone, and with a little more MDMA and a little less alcohol in the blood (Hernández-López et al., 2002). Feelings: a sedation score rose with alcohol alone but not with both drugs, where it stayed at the level of MDMA alone, and drowsiness ratings were lower with both drugs than with alcohol alone; ratings of feeling drunk rose with alcohol alone and with both drugs, with no significant difference between the two (at their peak about 58 with both drugs and about 40 with alcohol alone on a 100 mm line, editors' reading of the figure), and the authors conclude that MDMA reversed alcohol's sedation but did not reduce drunkenness; ratings of feeling high and stimulated rose with MDMA and with both drugs. Tests: on a timed symbol-matching test (digit symbol substitution), correct answers at the worst point fell by 9.0 with alcohol alone and by 8.11 with both drugs against the dummy (no significant difference between the two), but with both drugs the fall lasted about 1 hour (1 to 2 hours after the capsule) against 2 to 3 hours with alcohol alone, and over 6 hours it did not differ significantly from the dummy; decision time in a reaction test was slower than with the dummy at its peak only with both drugs, for about half an hour. Blood levels: MDMA peaked 13% higher with alcohol (260.29 against 231.42; p = 0.007), with no change in total exposure, and alcohol peaked 15% lower with MDMA (105.81 against 124.62 mg/dl; p = 0.004) and was 9% lower over 6 hours; the authors call these changes mild and within the range of differences between people. The MDMA levels are printed in mg/dl, which cannot be right for these values: the assay's stated range (25 to 400 ng/ml) points to ng/ml. Heart and body: the paper says cardiovascular, hormone and other physiological measures were taken but are not presented, and cites no paper that reports them, so it says nothing about what the mix does to heart rate or blood pressure (body temperature is not named among the measures); no serious adverse reaction occurred and all 9 finished. Nobody was asked how well they thought they were doing, and nobody drove: the authors' suggestion that people may feel they are doing better, or drive recklessly, is untested, and they say driving and field studies are needed. The men were healthy, experienced with MDMA, without past bad reactions to it, all with normal activity of a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) that breaks MDMA down, and given one amount of each drug once; women, people new to MDMA, other amounts, repeated doses, heat, dancing and crowds were not studied. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What happens when you mix MDMA with alcohol? In one lab study, 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four sessions a week apart: MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they did not know which. With both, the sleepy feeling that alcohol brought went away, but feeling drunk did not: if anything it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly so. On a timed symbol test, scores at the worst point fell about as much as with alcohol alone, though for about 1 hour instead of 2 to 3, and only with both drugs was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy. MDMA in the blood peaked 13% higher and alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Heart measurements were taken but never reported, so the study says nothing about the heart. Nobody asked the men how well they thought they were doing, and nobody drove. It was 9 men, one amount of each drug, in a quiet room.

statement: In 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30; at most 20 lifetime uses of psychedelics or MDMA) who each took MDMA (100 mg) and LSD (100 µg) at the same time, compared with each drug alone and with a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a calm hospital room (study conditions), the combination raised blood pressure and heart rate more than LSD alone, to about the levels of MDMA alone, but not body temperature, did not significantly lower the unwanted effects people rated on LSD, raised LSD's blood levels, and lowered and delayed MDMA's peak (Straumann et al., 2023). Heart and blood pressure (average of each person's highest value, ± SEM): systolic 150 ± 2.9 mmHg with both drugs against 137 ± 2.7 with LSD alone (p < 0.001), 148 ± 2.9 with MDMA alone (not significantly different) and 124 ± 2.4 with the dummy; diastolic 90 against 85 (p < 0.05), 89 and 77; heart rate 100 ± 3.6 beats a minute against 92 ± 4.5 (p < 0.05), 95 and 77. Temperature: 37.5 ± 0.08 °C with both drugs against 37.4 ± 0.06 with LSD alone (not significantly different), 37.3 with MDMA alone (lower than with both drugs, p < 0.05) and 37.0 with the dummy. Unwanted effects: complaint scores in the first 12 hours were 15 (± 2.2) with both drugs and 15 (± 1.9) with LSD alone (8.6 with MDMA alone, 1.9 with the dummy), and from 12 to 24 hours 5.5 against 3.1 (not significantly different); ratings of a bad drug effect (14 against 18 out of 100) and of fear (8.2 against 13) did not differ significantly from LSD alone; headache, lack of energy, loss of appetite and dry mouth were reported about as often with either drug or both; no severe adverse event occurred. On nausea the paper contradicts itself: its results say nausea on the complaint list was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD, its table shows nausea ratings lower with MDMA (7.9 out of 100) than with LSD (25) or both drugs (21), and its discussion says nausea was about as frequent with both drugs as with either alone; the item counts are in a supplement that was not read. Late in the LSD response the authors note trend-level, non-significant signs of lower well-being and more depressed mood with both drugs in some people. Blood levels: with MDMA, LSD's peak was 2.1 against 1.9 ng/mL (p < 0.05), its half-life 5.2 against 3.9 hours (p < 0.001) and its total exposure 19 against 14 ng·h/mL (p < 0.01; about a third more, editors' calculation); with LSD, MDMA's peak was 208 against 233 ng/mL (p < 0.001; about a tenth lower, editors' calculation) and came later, at 3.5 against 2.8 hours (p < 0.01), with total exposure unchanged; the paper's text and abstract mention only the change in LSD's levels. The authors attribute the higher LSD levels to MDMA blocking a liver enzyme (CYP2D6), which they inferred from other studies and did not measure. Their statement that they found no sign of greater serotonin toxicity rests on 24 healthy people given one pair of doses together in a calm room, which cannot show rare or setting-dependent harms; other doses, other timing, repeated doses, heat, dancing, alcohol or other drugs, and people with heart or psychiatric conditions or on interacting medicines were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: What if you take LSD and MDMA at the same time? In one lab study, 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days: LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which. With both, blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone: top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone, and heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was no higher than on LSD alone. Bad feelings, fear and the number of complaints were not clearly lower than on LSD alone, and on nausea the paper contradicts itself. The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later. Nobody had a serious problem, but this was one amount of each drug, taken together by healthy people in a calm hospital room, so it says little about rare dangers or about a party.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, block-randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data (card sc_straumann_2023: RoB 2 some concerns). Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective; the unwanted-effect scores and ratings are self-reports under imperfect blinding, allocation concealment is not described, most item-level statistics are in an unread supplement, the paper's three statements on nausea disagree, and the text leaves out LSD's effect on MDMA's levels.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one pair of doses taken together, healthy screened volunteers with limited drug experience, a calm hospital room, which the statement says; it claims nothing about party settings, other doses or timing, or rare harms.

imprecision.note: 24 people. The rises in blood pressure and heart rate against LSD alone are significant, but the findings that temperature and unwanted effects were no higher, or no lower, than with LSD alone are non-significant comparisons, not shown equivalence, and rare harms such as serotonin toxicity cannot be detected in 24 people.

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim leaves out how strong or long the good effects felt, and gives no timing.
